what_it_does: Large processors with many cores each have a last-level cache (LLC) — a big shared pool of fast on-chip memory that sits between the cores and the much slower main memory (RAM). To fit on chip, this cache is split into multiple independent 'slices,' one per region of the chip, and each slice makes its own decisions about which data to keep and which to evict. The best modern eviction policies (such as Hawkeye and Mockingjay) train a predictor by watching a sample of accesses, but each slice only watches its own local sample — it is blind to whether the same data was recently reused by other cores hitting a different slice. Drishti fixes this by letting each processor core's predictor train on data from all slices that core touches, giving it a global view of reuse without requiring extra wiring between slices. It also dynamically enlarges the sample of cache sets used for training within each slice, so the predictor sees enough accesses to make reliable predictions even when traffic is uneven.
